scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): grants that leisure is a worthy benefit, then argues it should not be technology's primary goal; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: New machines and tools constantly promise to save us time and effort.
Some people argue that the primary goal of technological advancement should be to increase efficiency so that people have more leisure time.
I agree that more leisure is a worthy benefit, but I do not believe it should be the primary goal of technology.

sections.role: Body 1 — Why leisure is a real benefit

sentences.text: First, using technology to free people for leisure is genuinely valuable.
Machines that handle dull or exhausting work can give people more time to rest and enjoy life.
For example, washing machines and dishwashers have freed countless hours once lost to household chores.
This shows that efficiency can improve daily life by leaving more room for family and relaxation.
People with more leisure can pursue hobbies, friendships, and interests that make life richer.
Rest and free time are also important for health and happiness, not mere luxuries.
To this extent, increasing leisure is a worthy aim for technology.

sections.role: Body 2 — Why it should not be the primary goal

sentences.text: Second, however, leisure should not be the single most important goal of technology.
Many of the greatest advances aim at saving lives, curing disease, or spreading knowledge.
Consider medical technology that heals the sick or clean-water systems that protect whole populations.
Such achievements matter far more than simply giving people extra free time.
Technology also connects people, expands education, and helps solve dangers like hunger and pollution.
Treating leisure as the chief goal would ignore these deeper and more urgent purposes.
Efficiency, then, is only one of the many good ends technology should serve.
In conclusion, using technology to give people more leisure is a real and worthwhile benefit.
But it is only one goal among many, and far from the most important.
The truest aim of technology is to improve human life as a whole, not merely to provide free time.
